extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research-integrity professionals, and readers interested in scientific misconduct and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and characterizing forms of fabricated or falsified content in scholarly publications (e.g., fake references, image manipulation, invented data or authors) and understanding how such issues lead to retractions and institutional sanctions. The page is a news-category listing illustrating real-world examples and patterns of research misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabricated references / hallucinated citations
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis of articles indexed in PubMed found that about one in 277 papers published in the first seven weeks of 2026 referenced a paper that didn’t exist. The researchers ... used AI to “distinguish genuine fabrications from formatting discrepancies such as informally abbreviated titles.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat non-existent citations as a distinct category of fabrication; be aware of a sharp increase since mid-2024 that coincided with the rise of AI writing tools. Detection may require automated methods (AI) that separate genuine fabrication from formatting/abbreviation inconsistencies. Monitor reports (e.g., Nature, Retraction Watch) about large numbers of potentially invalid references generated by LLMs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image falsification (figure manipulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A retraction notice states a joint research misconduct investigation determined 'falsification occurred during creation of figure S9C.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Image-level falsification uncovered by institutional investigations is a ground for retraction; journals and institutions may coordinate to request withdrawal when falsification in figures is confirmed. Look for investigation reports specifying which figure(s) were falsified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple items state that 'the data were fabricated' (e.g., papers retracted after investigations concluded the data were fabricated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabricated datasets are a primary basis for retraction. Detection often follows sleuthing (data audits, comparisons across papers) and institutional or journal inquiries. Retraction notices and institutional reports typically document the finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study not performed (false claim of conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper was retracted after an author told the journal the study had 'not actually been performed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explicit admission that experiments or studies were never carried out is a definitive basis for retraction, even many years after publication. Verify primary materials, protocols, and raw data when possible; author statements/communications can trigger formal retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fake authors and bogus institutions (sting/fabricated provenance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A published paper included fabricated authors, fabricated data, and a bogus institution (e.g., 'Simisai University' invented for a sting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers with invented author identities or affiliations indicate deliberate fraud; stings may create fake submissions to expose problems in peer review or editorial standards. Evaluate author affiliations and institutional legitimacy, and be alert to improbable author/institution details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author confession or admission of misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: A former graduate student wrote emails to an editor and co-authors confessing to misconduct in published papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author admissions (emails, communications) are actionable evidence that can lead to retraction and institutional investigations. Journals and institutions treat such confessions seriously and may coordinate to correct the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional findings and disciplinary sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions (e.g., Kyoto University) found researchers guilty of numerous counts of 'fraudulent activity' and imposed disciplinary dismissal; ORI concluded a researcher committed misconduct and imposed funding-related sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional investigations and national oversight bodies (e.g., ORI) are key authorities for determining misconduct and imposing sanctions (dismissal, degree revocation, funding prohibitions). Use institutional reports and notices to substantiate findings when evaluating a paper's integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data similarities / duplicated or recycled data across publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Sleuths discovered data similarities between a recently-retracted study and another by the same group, prompting further scrutiny and retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantial overlap or improbable similarities in datasets across different publications is a red flag for fabrication or duplication. Comparative data analysis and replication attempts are productive ways to surface such issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction notice content as documentary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notices often state specific reasons (e.g., 'falsification occurred,' 'data were fabricated') and note institutional actions (e.g., institutions alerted AAAS and requested the paper’s retraction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use retraction notices as primary sources that summarize findings, grounds for retraction, and institutional involvement. Evaluate the specificity and origin of claims within retraction notices when assessing the severity and nature of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of AI as both source of errors and detection tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Topaz’s group located the sharpest increase in hallucinated references in mid-2024, which they note coincided with the rise of AI writing tools. The researchers used AI to distinguish genuine fabrications from formatting discrepancies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that AI/LLMs can both generate invalid references and help detect them. When evaluating references, consider the possibility of AI-generated hallucinations and apply tools or human checks that can discriminate between formatting/abbreviation issues and fabricated citations.
